summary: Defines a Management Information Base module for managing linear protection in MPLS Transport Profile networks. It lets network management protocols such as SNMP configure and monitor that protection.

plainLanguage.summary: A dashboard with dials and switches lets an operator watch and control the backup lanes of a network.

subtitle: A management dashboard for backup paths in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Networks need a way to automatically switch traffic to backup paths when a failure occurs, and operators need tools to monitor and control this process.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8150 defines SNMP management objects that let operators configure and monitor linear protection domains with working and protection paths, control traffic switching between them, and receive alerts about network problems.
tldr.outcome: Operators can monitor MPLS-TP networks through a standard management interface, detect problems quickly, and let the network automatically protect traffic without manual intervention.

today: RFC 8150 is a Proposed Standard defining an SNMP MIB module for MPLS-TP linear protection management. It remains in active use by operators managing high-reliability transport networks that require automatic protection switching with centralized management visibility.

sections.title: Introduction to MPLS-TP Protection Management
sections.content:
RFC 8150 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing linear protection in MPLS-TP networks. An MIB is a collection of data objects that network devices expose through SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol, allowing operators to read and write configuration settings and status information.

This MIB specifically handles linear protection switching, which means automatic traffic rerouting between two paths when problems occur. It applies to MPLS-TP Label Switched Paths (LSPs), which are logical tunnels through the network that carry traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the instruction manual for a remote control that manages backup lanes in a network. It tells managers what buttons to press and what gauges to read.

sections.title: What Is Linear Protection
sections.content:
Linear protection is a method for protecting network traffic by using two separate paths between the same pair of endpoints. One is the working path, which carries traffic under normal conditions. The other is the protection path, which stands by to take traffic if something goes wrong.

When the system detects a fault or degradation on the working path, it automatically switches traffic to the protection path, minimizing service disruption. The RFC references two standard switching mechanisms: PSC (Protection State Coordination), defined in RFC 6378, and APS (Automatic Protection Switching), defined in RFC 7271. Both coordination modes ensure that both ends of the path switch at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two routes from your house to school. You normally take Route A. If Route A gets blocked, you automatically switch to Route B. The system tells both you and your friend at school at the same moment so you meet up correctly.

sections.title: Protection Types and Modes
sections.content:
The MIB defines several ways to set up protection. The bridge type determines how traffic is handled: in 1+1 protection, the source copies all traffic and sends it on both the working and protection paths simultaneously; at the destination, the receiver picks the best one and discards the other. In 1:1 protection, normally only the working path carries traffic, and the protection path remains idle until needed.

The switching scheme can be bidirectional or unidirectional. In bidirectional protection, if one direction of a path fails, both directions switch to the protection path. In unidirectional protection, each direction can switch independently if needed.

The switching behavior can also be revertive or non-revertive. In revertive mode, once the problem clears, traffic returns to the original working path after a wait timer. In non-revertive mode, traffic stays on the protection path once switched.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two styles: 1+1 is like sending two copies of your letter and the receiver picks the best one; 1:1 is like having a spare mailbox in case the main one breaks. Bidirectional means both lanes switch together; unidirectional means each can switch alone. Revertive means go back to the main lane after it's fixed; non-revertive means stay on the backup.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Tables
sections.content:
The MIB module organizes management objects into several tables. The mplsLpsConfigTable holds the configuration for protection domains, such as the domain name, mode (PSC or APS), protection type, and timing parameters like how long to wait before reverting to the working path.

The mplsLpsStatusTable mirrors the config table and holds the current runtime state of each domain, including which path is active and the current PSC state. The mplsLpsMeConfigTable associates each Maintenance Entity (ME)—a path being monitored—with its protection domain, marking it as either working or protection. The mplsLpsMeStatusTable holds the current protection status of each ME.

Beyond these tables, the MIB defines textual conventions for common data types. For example, MplsLpsReq represents the request fields in PSC control packets, encoding states like No Request, Manual Switch, Signal Fail, and Forced Switch. MplsLpsCommand allows management stations to trigger actions like switching, and MplsLpsState represents the internal state of the protection state machine.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has four filing cabinets: one for plans (config), one for what's happening right now (status), one for which paths exist (ME config), and one for how healthy each path is (ME status). It also defines a special language to describe switching commands and error states.

sections.title: Monitoring and Notifications
sections.content:
The MIB enables operators to monitor protection domains through read-only status objects. Operators can see which path is currently active, the time the protection domain has been in its current state, and fault/path information reported by the endpoints.

When important events occur, the MIB generates SNMP notifications (traps) to alert management stations. These include notifications for switchovers between working and protection paths, mismatches between endpoints in revertive mode or protection type, capability mismatches, protocol failures, and lack of response to switching requests.

The RFC specifies a 50 millisecond timeout for responses to traffic switchover requests and a protocol timeout of at least 3.5 times the PSC message interval. These timers ensure the network reacts quickly to failures without triggering false alarms due to transient network delays.
sections.plainLanguage: The management station can watch what's happening on each path and see which one has traffic. When something important changes—like a successful switch, a timeout, or a mismatch between the two ends—the system sends an alert message to the control room.

sections.title: Configuration and Control
sections.content:
Operators use the MIB to configure protection domains by creating entries in the config tables with parameters such as the protection mode (PSC or APS), protection type (1+1 vs 1:1, unidirectional vs bidirectional), and revertive behavior. Key timing parameters include the Wait-to-Restore timer (which delays reversion after a recovery, typically 5 to 12 minutes), the hold-off time (which delays switching to avoid thrashing when lower-layer protection is active), and the continual transmission interval for PSC packets.

The MIB also provides control objects to command protection switching. For example, an operator can issue a manual switch command to move traffic from working to protection (or back) for maintenance or testing. These write-accessible objects must be protected by SNMP security to prevent unauthorized modifications that could disrupt service.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator sets up a protection domain by filling in a form: how to protect (PSC or APS), what type (1+1 or 1:1), whether to go back to the main path when fixed, and various timers. The operator can also press a button to manually switch paths.

sections.title: Security and Standards Compliance
sections.content:
Because this MIB allows configuration and control of critical protection mechanisms, unauthorized access is a serious risk. The RFC emphasizes that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lack adequate security; SNMPv3 with User-based Security Model (USM) authentication and privacy is required. The document recommends using the AES cipher algorithm (RFC 3826) for encryption and mentions support for Transport Security Model (TSM) with SSH or TLS/DTLS as alternatives.

The MIB references related standards: RFC 3811 for MPLS MIB structure, RFC 6378 and RFC 7271 for the protection switching protocols, and RFC 7697 for MPLS OAM identifiers. Configuration objects are defined as read-write or read-create to maintain consistency with existing MPLS MIB modules, even though RFC 3812 no longer recommends SNMP SET for MPLS configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The system is locked down with strong passwords and encryption so only trusted operators can change settings. It follows rules set by other network protocols so it works smoothly with the rest of the network.
